nameStory: Three-petal bedstraw gets its name from its unique flowers, which typically have just three petal-like lobes instead of the four that most bedstraws display. The "bedstraw" part comes from the traditional use of these plants as mattress stuffing, since their tangled stems and leaves create a springy, fragrant bed when dried.
description: Three-petal bedstraw is a delicate, sprawling perennial that forms loose tangles of thin, wiry stems up to about 20 inches long. Its tiny linear to oval leaves grow in neat whorls around the stem, creating a ladder-like appearance. The plant produces clusters of small white or pale pink flowers, each with the distinctive three petal-like lobes that give it its name. This dainty wildflower often weaves through other vegetation, creating intricate green networks in wet areas.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white or pinkish flowers with three petal-like lobes instead of the typical four found on most bedstraws - this is the key identifying feature that sets it apart

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, narrow leaves arranged in whorls of 4-6 around the stem, creating a distinctive ladder-like pattern when viewed from above

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms loose, sprawling tangles of thin, weak stems that feel smooth and slightly sticky to the touch, often leaning on nearby plants for support

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Slender, square-shaped stems that are smooth and feel slightly rough when you run your finger backwards along them due to tiny backward-pointing bristles

habitat: Three-petal bedstraw thrives in wet areas throughout New England, particularly around marshes, pond edges, wet meadows, and boggy spots. You'll often find it growing in sphagnum moss or among sedges and rushes in areas that stay consistently moist. It also grows in wet ditches and along stream banks where the soil remains saturated for much of the growing season.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as the weather warms, with fresh green whorls of leaves appearing on last year's stems and new shoots sprouting from the base.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs from June through August, when the tiny three-petaled flowers are most visible among the tangled stems and bright green foliage.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and small fruits develop, while the foliage may turn yellowish before the first frost kills back the above-ground portions.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to the ground, leaving only the root system alive underground, though dried stem fragments may persist in protected areas.

funFact: Three-petal bedstraw is one of the most widely distributed plants on Earth, found on every continent except Antarctica and growing everywhere from Greenland's tundra to tropical mountains in Mexico - making it a true global citizen that somehow thrives in New England's wetlands!
confusionNotes: It's easily confused with other small bedstraws, but counting the flower petals is the foolproof way to identify it - if you see three petals instead of four, you've found three-petal bedstraw. Remember the rhyme: "Three petals three, that's the key!"
contextualKnowledge: The bedstraw family is actually part of the coffee family (Rubiaceae), which explains why some bedstraws have been used as coffee substitutes throughout history. Despite their delicate appearance, bedstraws are surprisingly tough plants that can handle harsh conditions.
compareHints: Unlike catchweed bedstraw which has sticky, grabby stems and four-petaled flowers, three-petal bedstraw feels smoother and has its distinctive three-petaled blooms. It's also much more tied to wet habitats than most other bedstraws, which tend to prefer drier soils. The consistently moist habitat preference and three-petaled flowers make it unmistakable once you know what to look for.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's bedstraws, catchweed is unique for its extremely clingy nature and annual growth habit.

Hedge bedstraw differs from other common bedstraws by its smooth stems and purely white flowers - catchweed bedstraw has sticky stems, lady's bedstraw has yellow flowers, and fragrant bedstraw has a sweet vanilla scent when crushed.
Unlike its weedy cousin catchweed bedstraw which grabs onto your clothes with hooked bristles, sweet woodruff stays put and feels soft to touch.
Among New England's bedstraws, fragrant bedstraw is unique for its sweet vanilla scent when crushed – most other bedstraws are odorless or have different scents.
Among New England's 15+ bedstraw species, licorice bedstraw stands out with its consistently four broad, oval leaves per whorl - most others have 6-8 narrow, linear leaves arranged in circles.
Marsh-bedstraw is distinguished from other bedstraws by its preference for consistently wet habitats and its delicate, mat-forming growth pattern.
Lady's bedstraw stands out among New England's bedstraws because of its bright yellow flowers - most other bedstraw species have white or greenish blooms.
Among New England's bedstraws, rough bedstraw is distinguished by its prominent stem hooks and preference for wet areas.
Unlike catchweed bedstraw with its velcro-like sticky stems or sweet woodruff's hay-like fragrance, Torrey's wild licorice has smooth stems and that distinctive taste.
Among the 15+ bedstraw species in New England, stiff marsh bedstraw is one of only two with 3-petaled flowers (the other being three-petal bedstraw).
Among New England's bedstraws, hairy bedstraw is unique for its consistently soft, fuzzy texture throughout the plant.

White bedstraw differs from other New England bedstraws by its upright growth habit and smooth stems - catchweed bedstraw has hooked bristles that grab onto clothing, while lady's bedstraw has bright yellow flowers instead of white.
Unlike the common catchweed bedstraw with its grabby, rough stems, boreal bedstraw is soft and non-sticky.
Northern bedstraw differs from other New England bedstraws by its upright growth habit and narrow leaves with three parallel veins.
Among New England's bedstraws, bluntleaf bedstraw stands out for its preference for wet habitats and those distinctive rounded leaf tips.
